headline: Citi turns constructive on renewables as Strait of Hormuz tensions highlight energy security value of non-fossil sources, with China's 50% renewable generation providing a blueprint.
reasoning: Gresham notes that renewables had been under pressure from US political rhetoric favouring fossil fuels, but the Strait of Hormuz situation has reminded investors that energy independence and security are critical. China's renewable buildout now accounts for around 50% of its energy production, and that diversification materially cushioned the impact of Middle East supply disruptions. In Australia, around 4 million households have adopted solar with a surge in household battery installations, highlighting the sector's momentum. Citi sees renewables as 'very interesting again' in the current environment.
quote: The Straits of Thomas has reminded us that energy independence is a huge source of energy. Security is a huge part of what we're seeing here. Um, over the last few years, China has led the way in renewable, uh, percentage of, of production of their energy, and they've ramped that up and it's around 50%. And if that hadn't been in place, the impact of the Straits of Hormuz, where they were getting about 20% of their energy need through that channel, would have been material. And so from our perspective, renewable is looking very interesting again. And, you know, we just need to look at Australia where sort of certainly interesting I think about 4 million households, uh, take up solar. And we've seen a huge resurgence, um, of battery household batteries.

headline: Citi warns cash is not a friend to investors in real return terms, urging deployment into risk assets to avoid missing rallies.
reasoning: Gresham notes that with inflation running as it is, cash does not generate real returns. He observes that since 2020, excluding the 2022 bear market, any ~3% correction has recovered in an average of 11 trading days, meaning investors risk missing rallies if they hold too much cash. The current investing base is primed to buy selloffs (FOMO dynamic), reinforcing the case to stay deployed.
quote: Your cash is not your friend here. Um, you've got with inflation, where it's running, you've got to look at real returns. And just to put that in context, if you if you go from 2020 through to date, um, and you take out the bare market of 2022, um, any sort of correction 3% down, um, has recovered on an average of 11 trading days. So we've got a sort of we've got an investing base that wants to buy a selloff. There is fear of missing out. And if you're going to sort of be conservative and sort of say, I need to have a cash in my portfolio, you're not getting paid for in real returns, and there's a real risk you're going to miss a rally.

headline: Citi holds gold as a core portfolio position, citing its negative correlation to equities and fixed income-like diversification properties.
reasoning: Gresham describes gold as a core position for Citi, noting it has behaved more like fixed income did 20 years ago — negatively correlated to equities — which makes it a genuine diversifier. As fixed income's correlation with equities has risen, gold has stepped in to play that role. He frames diversification as a key portfolio construction principle.
quote: gold is still a core position for us that has behaved more like fixed income 20 years ago. It's it's been negatively correlated. And from our perspective, diversification does remain key. You don't want to put all your eggs in one basket here.

headline: Citi positive on energy grid infrastructure as global annual investment needs to rise ~50% to ~$600bn to meet data centre and electrification demand.
reasoning: Gresham estimates global grid investment needs to grow from approximately $400bn to $600bn annually — a ~50% increase — to meet rising demand from data centres and broader infrastructure build-out. This makes anything tied to grid and electricity generation, including renewables with grid connectivity, an attractive area. Citi continues to like energy infrastructure within this context.
quote: anything around the grid and electricity generation, that renewable side has got a patch into the grid. So energy infrastructure continues to need, uh, by our estimation, sort of globally, probably another 50% annual spend from sort of 400 billion on grid investment to about 600 billion. In order to meet this increased demand of data centers and infrastructure. So that's an area that we continue to sort of like.

headline: Citi overweights cybersecurity as agentic AI dramatically accelerates breach timelines and enterprise security budgets double since 2010.
reasoning: Toby Gresham highlights that agentic AI has fundamentally changed the threat landscape, with breach-to-high-risk-data time falling from 98 minutes in 2021 to under 30 minutes as of last year per CrowdStrike research. Enterprise software budgets allocated to cybersecurity have doubled since 2010, a trend Citi expects to continue as AI makes attacks faster and easier. The cat-and-mouse dynamic between attackers and defenders means firms will keep spending more, making cybersecurity a core portfolio theme for Citi in H2.
quote: The argentea AI, um, has changed, you know, in a very short space of time, this opportunity set and as you said. Um, you know that example where one escaped from its sandbox? Um, and in a very short space of time, uh, obviously demonstrated that in a thirst for answering the question that was put to it, uh, it will go to quite nefarious means to do so. And, you know, a recent study out of CrowdStrike has sort of reminded us that back in 2021, it would take about 98 minutes for, um, a hack to get to high risk data. Uh, as of last year, that's down to about. It's under half an hour. And so from our perspective, although this is obviously a big concern, it is creating a lot of opportunity. And, you know, at the same time, we've seen I think since 2010 through to date, you've seen the percentage of budget that's being allocated by, um, uh, firms to their software has has doubled for cyber security. And so from our perspective, that that number is probably only going to go up as, as technology allows it to be easier and faster for, um, hacks to happen. But as a result, you know, in this game of cat and mouse, firms are going to spend more. So from our perspective, that's a really important theme for us to have in portfolios, and certainly for the second half of the year. That's a focus for us.

headline: Citi maintains equities as the best inflation-adjusted return asset class, with an overweight to US equities and AI as key themes.
reasoning: Gresham argues that given broadly positive global productivity dynamics, equities remain the best inflation-adjusted return. Citi is overweight US equities and specifically overweight AI, which represents a large portion of the US stock market. He frames this as the primary deployment destination for cash being moved into risk assets.
quote: equity is probably, you know, it is still the best inflation adjusted return. I mentioned that, you know we're overweight us on the theme side we're over also overweight AI. And you know that's a large part of the US equity stock market.

headline: Citi sees renewables as strategically attractive amid geopolitical energy security concerns, with economics reinforcing the case even where policy is unfavourable.
reasoning: Toby Gresham highlights that China's build-out of renewables to ~50% of energy production meaningfully cushioned the impact of Strait of Hormuz disruptions. In Australia, ~4 million households have solar and ~600,000 are storing energy via batteries, which helped drive a 12% decline in electricity prices in Q1. The Australian government is targeting 82% renewable by 2030, implying significant CapEx. Gresham argues that regardless of political headwinds in some countries, the economics of renewables and energy security imperative make the sector compelling.
quote: renewable is looking very interesting again. And, you know, we just need to look at Australia where sort of certainly interesting I think about 4 million households, uh, take up solar. And we've seen a huge resurgence, um, of battery household batteries. There's around 600,000 homes in Australia that are storing their energy now from that solar. And to sort of put you put in context how material that is. It was estimated that the first quarter of this year, electricity prices were down about 12% because of the fact that that electricity usage through solar by bike houses that do that take a big strain off the grid. And so, you know, I think under the current government, they're looking to get to 82% renewable and by 2030.

headline: Citi holds full overweight in US equities, viewing current AI CapEx cycle as sustainable and in the 'middle innings' with productivity feeding through to earnings.
reasoning: Gresham argues the current AI CapEx cycle is fundamentally different from the dot-com bubble because the bulk of S&P 500 companies are internally funding their capex, making it self-sustaining. Productivity gains from AI investment are already feeding through to the broader market. He also notes that the largest mega-cap tech spenders have seen multiple contraction rather than expansion, meaning cash flows are justifying valuations. Citi estimates roughly half the S&P 500 can be tied to AI-related themes, which underpins their largest equity overweight being in US equities.
quote: If the CapEx is going to be a strong focus. When we hear from some from Apple later this week and, and meta as well, and an understanding in that, you know, that the silicon names in the semicolons are benefiting from the scarcity and the prices going up. But, you know, the hyperscalers are going to have to buy these. And, you know, that's going to come at a broad cost. So a lot of it when we look at CapEx is how fundable is that. And actually if you look at certainly sort of Q1 of this year, um, the bulk of the S&P, uh, you know, a large part of it is internally funding this CapEx. And so, you know, this is very different from the internet bubble we saw previously where it wasn't sustainable. From our perspective, this CapEx spend is sustainable. And, you know, I think we'd also add on to that that it's feeding through to the numbers, because CapEx and the spend that we're seeing, you know, productivity is feeding through to the broad market. And I think from that perspective, another sign that would come through that this wasn't sustainable is if we looked at the PE of some of these larger mega cap tech stocks that were spending the most money. And the reality is, you know, into the tail end of this year and start of of sort of tail end of last year and the start of this year, we've actually seen some sort of multiple, um, contraction coming through, not multiple expansion. And so that the cash flow that these, these companies are throwing off, um, are actually justifying some of the valuations we're seeing. So from our perspective, we're comfortable. And this CapEx, we've sort of probably middle, middle innings through this band.

headline: Citi adding natural resources and energy names to portfolios as fixed income correlation with equities rises, with copper mines specifically highlighted.
reasoning: Gresham notes that fixed income has become increasingly correlated with equities, particularly in 2022, reducing its diversification benefit. As a result, Citi is bringing in natural resources and energy names to provide portfolio resilience and income. They are comfortable buying broad natural resources through ETFs, and copper mines are called out as specifically interesting.
quote: fixed income is something that we're looking at for, you know, portfolio resilience and income. But it's been increasingly correlated with equity, especially in 2022. So we're beginning to bring in those natural resources, bring in some of those energy names. Um, you know, we're happy to buy sort of more broad natural resources through ETFs. But, you know, copper mines look interesting to us as well.
